blocks.prompt: The Tree That Drinks With Its Feet
blocks.text: A tree has three big parts, and each one has a job. The roots grow under the ground. They hold the tree down so it does not fall over. They also drink water from the soil. The trunk holds the tree up. It is covered in bark, like a coat. Inside the trunk are tiny straws. Water goes up the straws to the leaves. The leaves are green. They catch sunlight and use it to make food for the tree. Roots drink. Trunk lifts. Leaves cook. Together they make a tree.

blocks.prompt: The Tree's Three Jobs
blocks.text: A tree looks like one thing, but it works like three machines joined together. Start underground. A tree's roots spread out wide, often wider than the branches above them, and most of them stay near the surface where the water is. Root hairs, so thin you need a microscope to see them, pull in water and the minerals dissolved in it. The roots also grip. That is why a tree can lean into a storm and stay standing. Next comes the trunk. Bark is the tree's skin, and it keeps out insects, fungus, and fire. Under the bark is a bundle of tiny tubes that carry water all the way up to the highest leaf. There is no pump. A tree has no heart. Water climbs anyway, every single day. At the top are the leaves. A leaf is a green kitchen. It takes in sunlight, water, and air, and it builds sugar. That sugar is the tree's food. It is also, slowly, the wood itself.

blocks.prompt: Inside the Trunk
blocks.text: Cut across a tree trunk and you do not find one solid material. You find layers, and every layer is doing a different job. The outside layer is bark: dead, corky, and there to keep out insects, fungus, and fire. Just inside the bark is the phloem, a set of tubes carrying sugar downward from the leaves to feed the branches, the trunk, and the roots, which cannot make food of their own. Under the phloem is the cambium, a layer so thin you could scrape past it without noticing, and it is the only part of the trunk that is actually growing. Every year the cambium lays new wood on its inside and new phloem on its outside. That is how a trunk gets thicker. Inside the cambium is the wood. The paler wood near the outside is sapwood, and it carries water upward from the roots to the leaves. The dark wood at the core is heartwood, and heartwood is dead. It has stopped carrying anything. It is packed with resin, and it does one job now: it holds the tree up. This is why an old tree can be hollow in the middle and still put out leaves every spring. Everything that matters is happening in the outer inch. Here is a stranger consequence. A trunk grows outward, not upward. Hammer a nail into a tree at four feet, walk away for fifty years, and the nail will still be at four feet. The tree got taller only at its tips.

blocks.prompt: How Water Climbs a Tree Without a Pump
blocks.text: A coast redwood lifts water more than 300 feet into the air, every day, with no pump, no heart, and no muscle anywhere in its body. For a long time nobody could explain it. The physics looked impossible, and yet the trees were standing right there doing it. The answer starts at the top, not the bottom. Every leaf is dotted with pores called stomata, which open to let in the carbon dioxide the leaf needs. Air is drier than the inside of a leaf, so while those pores are open, water escapes into the air. That loss is not the waste it appears to be. It is the engine. Water molecules cling to one another. Chemists call it cohesion, and in water it is unusually strong. So when one molecule evaporates out of a leaf, it tugs the molecule behind it, which tugs the one behind that, and the pull runs down an unbroken thread of water through narrow tubes of dead wood called xylem, all the way to the root hairs in the soil. The tree never pushes water upward. The dry air pulls, and the tree simply holds the straw steady. The roots do their own quiet work below. Their job is water and minerals, not food, because roots sit in the dark and cannot build sugar. Many trees hand part of that job to a partner. Threads of fungus wrap around the roots, reach further into the soil than any root hair could manage, and trade phosphorus and nitrogen for sugar the leaves made in the sun. Both sides come out ahead. This system has a ceiling. Pull a column of water too hard and it snaps, leaving an air bubble that can block that tube for good. That limit is one reason the tallest known tree, a redwood named Hyperion, stands at about 380 feet, and no tree anywhere stands at 500. Near the very top of a tall redwood the needles grow small and tough, living permanently on the edge of thirst, while the needles near the ground grow broad and soft. Same tree, two climates, 300 feet apart.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Most of a tree's mass comes from air, not soil
Van Helmont's willow, 1648: 164 pounds gained
Cohesion holds water in an unbroken thread
The cambium is only a few cells thick
Heartwood is dead: a mast, not a machine
Cut a ring of bark and the roots starve

blocks.prompt: The Tree That Eats Air
blocks.text: In 1648 a Flemish doctor named Jan Baptist van Helmont finished an experiment that had taken him five years. He had dried 200 pounds of soil, packed it into a pot, planted a willow shoot weighing five pounds, given it nothing but rainwater, and waited. At the end he pulled the willow out and weighed it: 169 pounds. Then he dried the soil again and weighed that. It had lost about two ounces. The willow had gained 164 pounds. The soil had given up almost nothing. Van Helmont concluded that the tree was made of water, which was wrong, but he had asked exactly the right question and proved something enormous: whatever a tree is built from, it is not mostly the ground it stands in. The real answer is stranger than his. A tree is built, in large part, out of air. Leaves open pores called stomata and take in carbon dioxide. Using the energy in sunlight, they split water, strip the carbon out of that carbon dioxide, and assemble sugar. Chains of those sugars become cellulose, and cellulose is the bulk of wood. The carbon in a fallen oak was drifting over your head not long ago. Soil supplies water and a short list of minerals. The mass, the trunk, the branches, the thing you can knock on, came mostly from the sky. That leaves the tree with a delivery problem, and this is where its parts stop being scenery and start being machinery. Water enters through root hairs, and through fungal threads that lace around the roots and reach where roots cannot, trading minerals for sugar. It then has to travel up, sometimes hundreds of feet, and the tree has no pump. So it cheats. As water evaporates from the open stomata, the molecules left behind are dragged after it, because water molecules cling to each other hard enough to be pulled in an unbroken thread. That thread runs through the xylem, narrow tubes of dead cells in the sapwood. The tree does not lift water. It lets the air pull, and holds on. Sugar has to travel the other way, down to roots that cannot feed themselves, and that traffic runs through the phloem, just inside the bark. Between xylem and phloem sits the cambium, a sleeve of living cells only a few cells thick. It is the entire growing trunk. Each year it lays new wood inward and new phloem outward, pale roomy cells in the fast of spring, dense dark cells as the season slows, which is why a stump reads like a barcode of its own weather. Two consequences follow, and both surprise people. First, most of a big trunk is dead. The heartwood at the core stopped conducting anything long ago. It is packed with resin and it works as a mast, not a machine, which is why a hollow tree can leaf out for another century: everything that matters is happening in the outer inch. Second, because the growing layer is a cylinder and not a base, trunks thicken but do not rise. Carve your initials at eye level and they will still be at eye level when you are old. The bark protects the whole arrangement, and its weakness is precise. Strip a ring of bark all the way around a trunk and you sever the phloem. The leaves go on making sugar. The roots never receive it. The roots starve, and then the leaves die of thirst, and it can take a year or more. The tree stands there the entire time looking exactly like a tree.
